newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan stocks end down on shooting, profit-taking.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan stocks end down on shooting, profit-taking.

text.p: Taiwan's brief bull run came to a halt on Thursday as stocks closed lower, hit by profit-taking after a dramatic recent rise and by shock at the gangland-style executions of six people in a Taiwan official's home.
The weighted index rose most of the morning, peaking at 6,771.39 but abruptly reversing direction in late trade as word of the Taoyuan shootings swept the market, brokers said.
At the close, the index had fallen 36.87 points or 0.55 percent at 6,692.98. Turnover was an active T$83.8 billion.
Brokers said the killings would rekindle concerns about Taiwan's poor social order and could chill market sentiment.
"The sort of incident always raises concerns, especially among investors," said Michael Hung of Nikko Securities.

Brokers said profit-taking was the key factor as investors seized on the shooting as a trigger for unloading some holdings. The market had risen dramatically since Monday and closed at a 22-month high on Wednesday, building pressure to sell.
Electronics outperformed other sectors, rising 0.84 percent despite the late selloff on word of big U.S. orders for 1997.
CMC Magnetics Corp, a leading videotape and computer disk maker, jumped T$1.6 or 3.65 percent to T$45.4 after the company said major new U.S. orders would push profits sharply higher.
Computer giant Acer Inc continued to attract strong buying on its bullish profit outlook, rising 80 Taiwan cents or 1.81 percent to T$45.

Shares in motherboard maker Asustek surged by the daily seven percent limit to end at T$171, surpassing Cathay Life at T$167 to become the market's "king share" -- the highest-priced stock in the market.
Asustek has been limit-up for seven straight sessions since its debut on November 14.
Wall Street's continued rise helped push shares higher at the open but not enough to withstand profit-taking pressure.

Brokers said the market got only a minor boost from the easing of restrictions on Thursday on foreign-owned equity in the local market, which was announced weeks ago and had been largely discounted. Foreign interests can now hold up to 25 percent of Taiwan share equity, up from 20 percent.
Despite the reform, many foreign funds have been selling down their Taiwan holdings for year-end window-dressing.
The market was likely to consolidate on Friday, brokers said, predicting a trading range of 6,680-6,800.
